lesson.title: Cross-Tabulating Two Categorical Variables
lesson.summary: A two-way table organizes counts for two categorical variables at once, using rows, columns, and totals to reveal how the variables relate.
lesson.body:
A single categorical variable, like favorite phone operating system, is easy to summarize: just count how many individuals fall into each category and list the counts in a simple frequency table. But many real questions involve two categorical variables measured on the same individuals at once, such as phone operating system and grade level, and a single frequency table cannot show how the two variables relate to each other. A two-way table, also called a contingency table, solves this by laying out counts for every combination of categories from both variables simultaneously, which is why statisticians say the table displays how one variable is contingent on the other.

In a two-way table, the categories of one variable label the rows and the categories of the other variable label the columns. Each interior cell holds the count of individuals who fall into that specific combination of row category and column category. Along the right edge and bottom edge of the table sit the row totals and column totals, often called marginal totals because they sit in the margins of the table, and the single number in the bottom right corner is the grand total, the count of every individual in the dataset. A table with r rows of categories and c columns of categories is sometimes called an r by c table, and the number of interior cells is simply r times c.

Suppose 300 students are surveyed about their grade level and their smartphone operating system. The results organize into this table: among 120 freshmen, 70 use an iPhone and 50 use Android; among 180 sophomores, 90 use an iPhone and 90 use Android. Reading across, the row totals are 120 for freshmen and 180 for sophomores, which sum to the grand total of 300. Reading down, the column totals are 160 for iPhone (70 plus 90) and 140 for Android (50 plus 90), which also sum to 300. Every count in the table, and every total, must be consistent with every other count: summing the row totals and summing the column totals must both land on the same grand total, which is a useful way to check your arithmetic before moving on.

Each cell answers a very specific question. The 70 in the freshman-iPhone cell does not mean 70 percent of anything; it means exactly 70 individual students are both freshmen and iPhone users. It is easy to confuse a cell count with a total, so always ask which group a number describes: is it counting people in one category, in one combination of two categories, or in the entire sample? Keeping that distinction straight is essential before you try to compute any percentage from the table, since every percentage you calculate later depends on choosing the correct count for both the numerator and the denominator.

A two-way table by itself is just an organized count, but it is the raw material for the next tools you will build: marginal distributions, which describe one variable alone using the totals in the margins, and conditional distributions, which describe one variable within a single row or column. Both of those tools are computed directly from the counts and totals you now know how to read from a table like this one, and both will reuse this same survey of 300 students throughout the rest of this unit.
